variants.headline: Both sides in sight near {{cityName}}
body: Our observers counted {{ourUnits}} of our regiments and {{theirUnits}} from {{opponent}} in the {{domain}} zone near {{cityName}}. If both sides stay in the area, either could contest the approaches. Whoever holds the ground and brings up support first will decide them.

variants.headline: The {{domain}} zone at {{cityName}}, entered
body: The observer's book lists {{ourUnits}} of our regiments and {{theirUnits}} from {{opponent}} in the {{domain}} zone at {{cityName}}. Our assessment was {{posture}}, and it weighs positions and support as much as the count. Who holds the approaches remains a question for the next entry.

variants.headline: What the count near {{cityName}} leaves out
body: The latest sighting places {{ourUnits}} of our regiments and {{theirUnits}} from {{opponent}} in the {{domain}} zone near {{cityName}}. Anyone reading the tally should ask who has the ground and who can bring up support. Neither answer is in the ledger, and until one is, the approaches belong to whoever moves first.

variants.headline: Barbarians in sight of {{cityName}}
body: Smoke from the raiders' fires has been rising beyond the ridge above {{cityName}}, and the watch counts {{barbarians}} of them. The last farm outside the wall was abandoned at midday, its door still open. The garrison has shut the north gate and sent for help.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Raiders at the walls
body: Raiders on the ridge! {{barbarians}} of them, and the watch has seen their fires! Drive the herds inside and bar every shutter! Let no child stray past the gate! We hold the wall! We hold the wall!

variants.headline: The herdsmen reach {{cityName}} without the herds
body: The farmer's cart came through the gate at a gallop with an empty harness trailing behind it. Raiders are camped near {{cityName}}, {{barbarians}} by the watch's count, and the ridge glows with their fires each night. 'The oxen bolted before I did,' the farmer said. 'I did not wait to argue.'

variants.headline: Counting raiders at {{cityName}}
body: The watch has fixed a figure on the raiders around {{cityName}}: {{barbarians}}. A band of that size must scatter to feed itself, which means the farms outside the wall will suffer before the town does. Driving them off is a bill the harvest can barely cover, and the town will pay it in grain either way.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, the garrison answers: {{posture}}
body: {{cityName}}'s town book lists raiders in the fields, {{barbarians}} by the watch's count. The captain's answer is written in the margin: {{posture}}. That evening the outer farms were emptied and the gate was barred before the stars appeared.

variants.headline: {{city}} goes hungry under siege
body: Food in {{city}} is running short, and the siege has begun to show at every table. A porter at the grain exchange says the sacks now weigh less than their labels promise. The city is counting meals by the week, and the count is falling.

variants.headline: Who can still buy supper in {{city}}?
body: Hunger in {{city}} falls harder on some tables than others. The families who buy flour daily will feel the siege first, while a merchant with a full cellar can wait a month. The stalls still stand, but coin gives out before grain, and when the last purse is empty the stalls will go with it.

variants.headline: In {{city}}, the queue starts before dawn
body: {{terms.civic.people}} of {{city}}, the baker has begun cutting loaves smaller and saying nothing about it. The queue forms before dawn, and every customer watches the scale. Ask him how long the flour will last, and he answers by tapping the empty barrel behind the counter.

variants.headline: To the faithful of {{city}}: hold fast
body: To the faithful in {{city}}: the granaries are nearly bare and the gates must remain shut. Throw open the shrines to anyone without a warm room, and share what bread you can spare. The season will turn, and what is given now will not be forgotten.

variants.headline: The walls of {{cityName}} are failing
body: Half of the wall of {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, is down, and its rubble lies in the streets. A carter who passed beneath the gate said he could see the sky through the breach. The defenders have not begun repairs, which suggests they have given up on the outer wall.

variants.headline: An accounting of {{cityName}}
body: City examined: {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}.
Wall standing: half of it at best.
Verdict: the next storm will finish what the siege began.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight: heavy damage at {{cityName}}
body: Word from abroad tonight: half of {{cityName}}'s wall, held by {{civilization}}, is down. Engineers say the breach is wide enough to march through. The city still flies its flag, but the stone no longer argues for it.

variants.headline: The walls of a rival come down
body: {{cityName}} belongs to {{civilization}}, and half of its wall is down. Stone in that condition turns a battle into a question of nerve, because the defenders must now choose where to make their fight. If {{civilization}} has a reserve, this is the week to show it.

variants.headline: The reading at {{cityName}} changes to {{posture}}
body: On turn {{observedTurn}}, our assessment of the {{domain}} zone at {{cityName}} changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. {{civilization}} holds the city, and the new word tells our observers to expect an assault to open there. The roads around {{cityName}} will be worth watching in the days ahead.

variants.headline: From {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} at {{cityName}}
body: The front assessment for {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The reading covers the {{domain}} zone, and it turned offensive before any formation was seen to move. If the balance our observers measured holds, the next days should show the assault itself.

variants.headline: Turn {{observedTurn}}: the entry for {{cityName}}
body: In the campaign record, turn {{observedTurn}} marks a change from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} in our assessment of the {{domain}} zone at {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}. The cause is unrecorded.

variants.headline: A new word on the board at {{cityName}}
body: The watch board's entry for {{cityName}} on turn {{observedTurn}} went from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. That is our command's assessment of the {{domain}} zone. What happened on the ground is still an open question.

variants.headline: The entry at {{cityName}} moves from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}
body: Our front assessment for {{cityName}} moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The earlier word described a withdrawal, and the new one describes a force back on its footing in the {{domain}} zone. The city is held by {{civilization}}, and the next sighting will show whether the pause ends in a settle or a fresh advance.

variants.headline: After the withdrawal: the reading at {{cityName}}
body: The entry for {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The shift ends a stretch in which the {{domain}} zone was read as a withdrawal, and it looks like a threat putting itself back in order. Our posts along that front should stop counting on the quiet.

variants.headline: The board at {{cityName}} is updated
body: The front board for {{cityName}} was updated on turn {{observedTurn}}. The reading moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} in the {{domain}} zone, and the city is held by {{civilization}}. In plain words: the force our watchers saw pulling back has stopped and is being put in order again.

variants.headline: A different word for the same ground at {{cityName}}
body: The map room has changed its entry for {{cityName}} from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, dated turn {{observedTurn}}. A change of that kind is a judgment about the {{domain}} zone, and readers who follow the front will want it explained in plain language. The {{terms.civic.government}} should say what the new word means and how long it expects the reading to stand.

variants.headline: The reading at {{cityName}} turns to {{posture}}
body: Our staff entered a new front reading for {{cityName}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The {{domain}} entry moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and the city is held by {{civilization}}. The new word means the pressure on that front has eased, though the next sighting will show how long it stays that way.

variants.headline: The new word at {{cityName}}, and the questions it raises
body: The front entry for {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. A withdrawal reading is a statement about the balance our observers can see in the {{domain}} zone, and it invites questions about what happens next. The public has been given the label and nothing more.

variants.headline: A change in the {{domain}} entry at {{cityName}}
body: We are informed that the front entry for {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, passed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The dispatch supplies the new word and no commentary. We print the change as it reached us and leave the explanation to those who keep the board.

variants.headline: The word at the carters' stand: {{cityName}}
body: At the carters' stand, a man read the day's board aloud for those who cannot: {{cityName}}, turn {{observedTurn}}, {{posture}} where the last entry said {{previousPosture}}. Someone asked whether the new word meant the fighting had stopped. Nobody at the stand could answer, and the reader moved on to the next line.

variants.headline: Enemy colors near {{cityName}}
body: Columns under the banners of {{enemies}} have been seen a short march from {{cityName}}. Watchmen counted their fires after nightfall, and the miller has hauled his flour behind the wall. The roads remain open, though the carts that use them have grown scarce.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! The enemy is near
body: Look to the north road! Soldiers of {{enemies}} are coming, and their fires already light the ridge! Bring in the flocks and shut the shutters! No one walks the fields after dark! Pass the word! Pass the word!

variants.headline: Three things an army near {{cityName}} can do
body: A force flying the colors of {{enemies}} has come within a day of {{cityName}}. This is more men than a raiding party needs, which leaves three uses: a siege, a march through the fields, or a screen while the real blow falls elsewhere. Our officers should be asking which, not merely counting.

variants.headline: Enemy troops just showed up near {{cityName}}
body: Enemy troops near the city. Banners: {{enemies}}. Close enough that the watch can name them.

variants.headline: {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed in the field
body: The latest fighting cost {{victim}} {{count|regiment|regiments}}, every one of them marching under the same standard. Our soldiers have stacked the captured colors beside the gate, and the pile reaches a man's shoulder. {{victim}} will need a season to replace what fell in an afternoon.

variants.headline: The enemy's losses, counted
body: {{victim}} regiments destroyed: {{count}}.
Standards taken: one design, repeated.
Balance of the season: entered in our favor.

variants.headline: {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed in the fighting
body: From the front tonight: our troops have destroyed {{count|regiment|regiments}} of {{victim}}. Every one of them marched under the same flag, and that flag now hangs in our camp. A season of recruiting will not replace what an afternoon took.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed
body: Gather and hear the count! {{count}} regiments of {{victim}} are broken on the field! Their banners fill a cart, and their families will learn the number soon enough! Tell it in the square and sing it in every tavern!

variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{winner}}
body: News has come that {{winner}} has taken {{cityName}}, the capital of {{loser}}, by force, {{distance}} from the nearest of our cities. The report arrived with a ship's cargo, and the customs clerk read it twice before entering the duty. The war is far away, but the prices it moves are not.

variants.headline: After {{cityName}} falls, where do the envoys go?
body: {{cityName}}, the seat of {{loser}}, now answers to {{winner}}. A state can lose its capital and keep its authority, or keep the buildings and lose the habit of command. Watch which envoys still call at which door, and the answer will show itself.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital
body: The year's record states that {{winner}} took by arms {{cityName}}, the capital of {{loser}}, at a distance of {{distance}} from our own cities. The keeper of the rolls entered the fall beside the accounts of plague and drought. Prayer was ordered for the city's people, and no cause was written.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight: {{cityName}} falls
body: Abroad tonight, {{winner}} has seized {{cityName}}, the capital of {{loser}}. The city lies {{distance}} from the closest of our cities. New maps will be needed by morning, and the embassies will be busy before the week ends.

variants.headline: A capital falls near our own border
body: A capital has fallen near our border: {{winner}} has taken {{capitalDescription}}. Refugees have already been seen on the road, carrying what they could tie to a cart. Our frontier posts are counting them as they pass.

variants.headline: What {{winner}}'s capture means here
body: When {{winner}} took {{capitalDescription}}, it gained more than buildings. It gained the offices, the archives and the habit of obedience that gather in a capital. The question now is whether the displaced government can rule from another city.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital near our borders
body: The annals record that {{winner}} captured {{capitalDescription}} in this year. The court scribe wrote the entry in a steady hand and left a space beside it for the terms. That space remains empty, and the border has been quiet since.

variants.headline: A capital just fell near us
body: Capital down: {{winner}} has taken {{capitalDescription}}. It is close to us. Watch the roads.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} changes hands near our border
body: {{cityName}}, a town near our border, has changed hands. {{winner}} took it from {{loser}}, and the fighting took place {{distance}} from our own fields. A different banner hung over its gate by evening. Our patrols have been told to hold their line and watch.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{winner}}
body: {{cityName}} has passed from {{loser}} to {{winner}}, at a distance of {{distance}} from our border. A town that close is a market, a road junction and a warning, depending on who holds it. The flag has changed; the garrison {{winner}} leaves behind will decide the road and the market in the seasons ahead.

variants.headline: Notice from abroad: {{cityName}}
body: Notice is given that {{cityName}}, formerly held by {{loser}}, {{distance}} from our frontier, is now held by {{winner}}. Travelers should expect new guards and new questions at its gate. Merchants with goods in its warehouses should present their papers before the week is out.

variants.headline: A new flag {{distance}} out
body: {{distance}} from our farms, the flag over {{cityName}} has changed. {{winner}} took it from {{loser}}, and the market opened the next morning as if nothing had happened. The stallholders have seen conquerors before.

variants.headline: {{neighbor}}'s army now outranks ours
body: The army of {{neighbor}} now outnumbers ours, according to the count kept at the war office. The clerks ran the figures twice before sending them up. No one there would say the gap is small.

variants.headline: The tally of arms
body: Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
The balance: theirs, for the first time this season.

variants.headline: Ask why {{neighbor}}'s army passed ours
body: {{neighbor}} has passed us in the count of arms, and the {{terms.civic.government}} has not explained how. The {{terms.civic.people}} pay for every regiment we raise, and they are entitled to know what our money bought. Either the count is wrong or the policy is.

variants.headline: The balance of arms has turned
body: In this season the army of {{neighbor}} exceeded our own in number. The war office entered the change without comment, as it enters the weather. The frontier regiments were ordered to stand their ground and report.

variants.headline: Our army passes {{neighbor}}'s
body: The war office count now puts our army above {{neighbor}}'s. The new figure was posted on the board, and an officer stood looking at it longer than the others. He said only that the lead would have to be used before it was spent.

variants.headline: Our arms in good order
body: Letters from the war office state that our forces now exceed those of {{neighbor}} in the field. The return was read at the war office and entered without ceremony. A lead in numbers is a tool; what matters is the hand that holds it.

variants.headline: Our army just passed {{neighbor}}'s
body: Count changed: our army is bigger than {{neighbor}}'s now. The board at the war office says so. Somebody should tell the enemy.

variants.headline: The account of strength
body: Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
The balance: ours, by the difference.

variants.headline: {{city}} takes heavy damage
body: The walls of {{city}} have been badly hit, and one stretch of stone has come down altogether. Dust from the breach has settled on the roofs as far as the market square. The garrison has moved its stores underground and posted extra men at the gap.

variants.headline: The cost to {{city}}
body: The walls of {{city}} have lost a quarter or more of what they were built to bear, and that is not enough for comfort. A breach changes the arithmetic of a siege: the defender must now watch two lines, the wall and the hole in it. Every hour spent repairing is an hour the attacker also gets to use.

variants.headline: The crack in {{city}}'s wall
body: A mason walked the length of the wall at {{city}} this morning, tapping the stone with a mallet and saying nothing. Where he struck, the stone rang hollow, and he has asked for lime and a second cart. His apprentice says the old man has not slept since the first strike.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{city}}! The walls are hurt
body: Stand clear of the wall! The stone is cracked and loose overhead! Keep the children off the rubble and let the masons work! We will mend it, but not if you stand in the way!

variants.headline: Our front at {{cityName}} is read as {{posture}}
body: Our own observers entered a new reading for the front at {{cityName}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The {{domain}} entry moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and the city is ours. The new word means our staff sees an opening around the walls and intends to strike into it.

variants.headline: From {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} at {{cityName}}
body: The front assessment for {{cityName}} changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. A counterattack reading says our observers see an opening in the {{domain}} zone. Openings of that kind do not wait, and the staff that called for the counter has a short season to use it.

variants.headline: A change on the board at {{cityName}}
body: The front board for {{cityName}} shows a new entry tonight, dated turn {{observedTurn}}. The reading moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} in the {{domain}} zone. The force that dug in around the city now means to come out and strike.

variants.headline: Our line at {{cityName}} is read anew
body: Dispatches from the map room state that the front at {{cityName}} has been reassessed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, with the change entered on turn {{observedTurn}}. The dispatch describes the {{domain}} zone and offers no forecast. We print the entry as it stands.

variants.headline: The front at {{cityName}} is read as {{posture}}
body: Our observers entered a new front reading for {{cityName}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The {{domain}} entry moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and the city is ours. The new word means the staff wants the force around it dug in and holding its ground.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, a quieter word on the board
body: The front entry for {{cityName}} moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}} on turn {{observedTurn}}. The dispatch gives the new reading for the {{domain}} zone and no explanation of what prompted it. Our readers may judge for themselves whether the change follows the ground or the mood at headquarters.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! The board has a new word
body: The watch board at {{cityName}} has a fresh entry, dated turn {{observedTurn}}. The word for the {{domain}} zone is now {{posture}}, where the last entry said {{previousPosture}}. Ask at the gate for the full notice, and keep the streets clear for the runners.

variants.headline: The record of {{cityName}}'s front
body: In this season the front book for {{cityName}} passed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The change is dated turn {{observedTurn}} and concerns the {{domain}} zone. The scribe records the new reading and adds no interpretation.

variants.headline: {{count}} of our regiments lost in action
body: The latest fighting with {{killer}} cost us {{count|regiment|regiments}}. The news reached the war office in a single dispatch, and the clerk who copied it left the room without speaking. The lists of names will take longer to prepare than the count did.

variants.headline: Our losses, counted
body: Regiments lost to {{killer}}: {{count}}.
Names entered: still being copied.
The account: not yet closed.

variants.headline: The empty bunks
body: At the barracks, the sergeant walked down the row of bunks and did not stop at {{count|regiment|regiments}} of them, every one lost to {{killer}}. The blankets are folded and the kits are gone, and he has not yet asked for replacements. He says the room is quieter than it used to be.

variants.headline: The count from the fighting
body: They say {{killer}} took {{count}} of our regiments. I heard it from a man who was there, and he would not say more than the number. The families will hear the rest soon enough.
